newsitem.title: USA: U.S. enters seventh years of growth.
newsitem.headline: U.S. enters seventh years of growth.

text.p: How long can the good times keep rolling? That's what many Americans would like to know as the U.S. economy enters its seventh straight year of growth next month.

From all appearances, the United States is leading a charmed economic life. It is the envy of the industrial world in job creation. Inflation was so low that in January, there was virtually none at all. The economy is not booming but growing steadily, having expanded by 2.4 percent last year.
The United States is enjoying its third-longest economic expansion since World War II, taking a back seat only to the heady 1960s and the go-go 1980s.

"I don't see anything in the near term that will cause the expansion to end and a recession to start," said Larry Chimerine, managing director at the Economic Strategy Institute, a non-profit Washington think-tank.
"It wouldn't shock me if it went on this way with moderate growth for a couple more years at least," he said.

That's the consensus view. The latest Blue Chip survey of leading business economists predicted the economy would continue its steady but moderate growth, expanding by 2.5 percent in 1997 and 2 percent in 1998.

"My own guess is that this can go on for quite a while. I don't see imbalances in the economy. I don't see any of the traditional early warning signs of recession," said Randell Moore, executive editor of Blue Chip newsletter.
Many things are credited with keeping the expansion going. Some say the growth of world trade has helped.

Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan likes to stress that the business cycle is not dead, but concedes that structural changes, such as better inventory control, have made the economy more efficient at moving goods and services and may be helping prolong growth.
But Greenspan has also warned against over-confidence. He is clearly worried that "irrational exuberance" in the U.S. stock market could end up harming the economy.
Others note that times were better in the past -- such as in the 1950s and 1960s -- but recession still returned.

"The fact that it (recession) did not occur for six years in the United States is a very good thing, but it is not something someone should place bets on," said Victor Zarnowitz, director of Columbia University's Centre for International Business Cycle Research.

Anthony Chan, chief economist at Banc One Investment Advisers in Columbus, Ohio, said he was so "obsessed" with the current high levels of credit-card debt that he worries there could even be a U.S. recession next year.

"I think the seeds of the destruction of this expansion are still not clear on the radar screen," Chan said. "But I think that high levels of consumer credit offer the possibility of something that could go wrong."

The last recession, in 1990-91, was relatively mild, and the early part of the recovery starting in April 1991 was so slight many people didn't notice it. Employment was so slack that the period became known as the "jobless recovery."

In 1992, Bill Clinton was able to campaign for the White House on the economy's weakness even though it was technically out of recession. He was safely elected before it was known that the economy actually had grown that year by 2.7 percent.
Growth has been moderate throughout the expansion, averaging about 2.6 percent -- much less than the nearly 5 percent average growth rate of 1960s and 1980s expansions, Chan said.

Much is riding on continued economic growth. Those who want to balance the federal budget are counting on it. The White House and Congressional Budget Office forecast economic expansion for several years to come.

"Most recent expansions have ended because of rising inflation, financial imbalances, or inventory overhangs. None of these conditions exists at present," the Economic Report of the President said last month.
Chan thinks he has found a problem. Consumer credit as a percentage of personal income is near record levels, around 18 percent, he said.

But in recent months banks have started to tighten their lending standards for consumer credit again. Since much of the growth in consumption has been financed by debt, reforming lending standards could slow consumption and therefore the economy, Chan said.
"I think a recession is a possibility in the first half of 1998," he said.
Greenspan recently made clear the central bank was concerned about the run-up in stock prices because it could be a harbinger of faster inflation and could damage the economy if it abruptly reversed.
"If we allow inflationary imbalances to start to emerge, history tells us that the end of the expansion is near at hand," Greenspan said Feb.26.
